# California Security Deposit Review

You have a few tenant-rights issues to check: whether the landlord’s deductions are for ordinary wear and tear, whether the move-out timing and notice were handled correctly, and whether the deposit accounting was provided on time and in detail.

## Tenant Rights Issues to Review

- **Security deposit limit and handling**
  - California generally limits residential security deposits and requires proper return of the unused portion after move-out.
- **Ordinary wear and tear vs. damage**
  - Repainting and carpet cleaning are often disputed if the apartment had only normal use and no unusual damage.
- **Reasonable deduction standard**
  - The landlord should only deduct amounts tied to actual, documented cleaning or repair needed beyond normal wear.
- **Itemized statement requirement**
  - If deductions were taken, you can review whether the landlord provided an itemized explanation and supporting receipts or estimates where required.
- **Move-out notice and lease end date**
  - Your 30 days’ notice may matter for lease timing, but it does not automatically justify deposit deductions.
- **Move-out inspection / photos**
  - If there was a pre-move-out inspection or documented condition report, it can help show whether the charges were fair.
- **Deadline to return deposit**
  - Check whether the deposit return and statement were sent within California’s required timeframe after you vacated.

## Documents to Gather

- Signed lease and any addenda
- Proof of security deposit payment for **USD 2,400**
- Your 30-day notice and proof of delivery
- Move-in condition report, photos, and video
- Move-out condition report, photos, and video
- Any email/text messages with the landlord about condition, repairs, or deductions
- The landlord’s itemized deduction statement
- Receipts, invoices, or estimates for repainting and carpet cleaning
- Any forwarding address you provided
- Proof of the date you surrendered possession and keys

## Neutral Issue Checklist

| Issue | What to Check | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| Deposit return timing | When the deposit and statement were sent after move-out | Late return can strengthen your claim |
| Itemization | Whether deductions were listed clearly and specifically | Vague charges are easier to dispute |
| Wear and tear | Whether repainting/carpet cleaning were due to normal use only | Normal wear is generally not chargeable |
| Actual cost proof | Whether the landlord has receipts or estimates | Deductions should match real costs |
| Pre-existing condition | Whether the unit had similar wear at move-in | Helps show the charges were not caused by you |
| Notice and surrender date | Whether your notice and move-out date were documented | Confirms the lease timeline and possession date |
| Photos and inspections | Whether both sides documented condition | Strong evidence for or against deductions |

## Draft Message Requesting Itemized Deposit Return

Subject: Request for Itemized Security Deposit Return

Hello [Landlord/Property Manager Name],

I am writing regarding my security deposit for the apartment I leased from 2025-02-01 through my move-out on 2026-01-15.

I understand you are withholding USD 900 for repainting and carpet cleaning. Based on the condition of the apartment at move-out, I believe the unit showed only normal wear and tear and no major damage. Please send me:

- A full itemized statement of all deductions
- Copies of receipts, invoices, or estimates supporting each charge
- A clear explanation of how each deduction relates to damage beyond normal wear and tear
- The remaining balance of my security deposit, if any

Please also confirm the date you consider the tenancy ended and the date the deposit accounting was mailed or sent.

I would appreciate a written response within 10 business days. Thank you for your time and attention.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]
[Forwarding Address]
[Email / Phone]
